title: Q (worked example): Find the specific heat capacity of a metal piece dropped into water
topicTitle: Measurement of specific heat capacity of solids and liquids
notes: **Setup:** a 200 g metal piece at 100Â°C is dropped into 500 g of water at 25Â°C (calorimeter heat capacity negligible). Final temperature is 30Â°C. (c_water = 4200 J/kgÂ·K)
By the principle of calorimetry: Heat lost by metal = Heat gained by water

In a mixture, heat lost by the hot metal equals heat gained by the cooler water if the cup and the room are ignored. Forgetting the cup makes the metal's specific heat come out too small, because some of the metal's heat warmed the cup and was blamed on a smaller c.
The working relations are Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water and c = Q / (m Δθ). Name each symbol, convert the data into SI units, and only then substitute.

A 0.20 kg metal piece at 100°C is dropped into 0.50 kg of water at 25°C. The final temperature is 30°C. The cup is neglected and c_water = 4200. Find c. Heat lost = 0.20 × c × (100 − 30). Heat gained = 0.50 × 4200 × (30 − 25).
0.20 × c × 70 = 10500. 14 c = 10500, so c = 750 J/kg K. Including a cold cup would raise this calculated c, because the metal would have supplied extra heat.
The result is 750 J/kg K.. Check it by substituting back into Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water and confirming the units.
